records.place: De Rust farm, Elgin district, Cape South Coast region

wine.name: Seven Flags Chardonnay
wine.sites: The two oldest Chardonnay blocks on De Rust, planted in 1987 and by the house's account among the oldest vines of Elgin, on south facing slopes planted to clones 175 and 270.
wine.making: Fermented with the cellar's own wild yeasts, never inoculated, in a selection of French oak barrels, a modest share of them new, and then left in barrel for about nine months, with restrained work on the lees, before the barrels are blended and bottled.
wine.glass: Lemon, lime and Granny Smith apple with pear and white peach, a flinty, struck match reduction, oatmeal and a light nuttiness, held by fresh acidity and a chalky, salty finish.
wine.ageing: Tight in its first years, it opens after three or four years in bottle and keeps for a decade in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle gains from air; a Burgundy white glass.

label.means: The house's name for a Chardonnay and a Pinot Noir from its older vines.
Grown in the Elgin district of the Cape South Coast region.

records.table: Paul Cluver is the family farm where, by two accounts, Elgin's first commercial vines went in, and Seven Flags Chardonnay comes from those blocks of 1987, wild fermented in French oak. Expect lemon, green apple and flint on a cool, chalky line.
records.story: The Cluver family began farming De Rust, high in the Elgin valley, in 1896, and for most of the century that followed the farm was known for apples grown for export. In the mid 1980s Stellenbosch Farmers Winery proposed a joint venture: the family would give the land and the water, the company the technical training and supervision. The soils, aspects and climate zones of the farm were mapped, and the first commercial vineyards of Elgin went in on De Rust in 1987 by the house's account, in 1986 by another. The family later went on alone, ending the venture, and built a cellar of its own on the farm. Its two leading wines took the name Seven Flags: the Pinot Noir came first, with the 2006 vintage, and the Chardonnay followed with the 2014 vintage, drawn from the vines of 1987, by then some twenty seven years old. Those blocks are the old heart of a district young in wine. The Seven Flags Chardonnay is Elgin's story told in one glass: an apple farm turned wine estate, where old vines, height and a slow, cool season give Chardonnay of tension rather than weight.

others.name: Paul Cluver Estate Chardonnay
others.note: The estate Chardonnay below Seven Flags, wild fermented in French oak barrels from several blocks of De Rust.

others.name: Seven Flags Pinot Noir
others.note: The Pinot Noir of the Seven Flags pair, first made with the 2006 vintage.

others.name: Paul Cluver Riesling
others.note: The house is known in the Cape for Riesling, dry and sweet, including a Noble Late Harvest.

traps: Seven Flags names two wines, a Chardonnay and a Pinot Noir; the Pinot Noir came first, with 2006, and the Chardonnay only with 2014.
The Seven Flags Chardonnay comes from the two oldest blocks of the farm; the Estate Chardonnay is the wider wine beneath it.

cards.front: Paul Cluver Seven Flags Chardonnay: from which vines does it come?
cards.back: The two oldest Chardonnay blocks on De Rust, planted in 1987.

With cultured yeast in stainless steel tanks
In concrete eggs with no oak at all
In large old casks of Slavonian oak
questions.exp: The house ferments it without inoculation in a selection of French barrels, a modest share new; it is neither a tank wine nor a large cask wine.

questions.q: With which vintage did Paul Cluver first release a Seven Flags Chardonnay?
questions.exp: The Chardonnay joined the tier with 2014; 2006 is the first Seven Flags Pinot Noir, 1987 the planting of its vines and 1896 the family's arrival on De Rust.

report: The house spells itself Clüver; the plan's Paul Cluver is kept for the producer and the prose, and the founder, who is living, is never named beyond the house's name.

The first planting is 1987 on the house's vineyard page and in a winery guide, 1986 on the Wines of Elgin page for the founder (whose address carries a living name, so it is not listed), and the story gives both.

The maiden wine (a Riesling of 1990 made at Nederburg, or a first bottling of 1991), the end of the joint venture and the new cellar in 1996, and the first estate vintage of 1996 each rest on one source and are left undated; the story says only that the family later went on alone and built its own cellar.
What the seven flags stand for was not found in any source and is left out.

The oak is 36 per cent new for 2021 on the house's sheet and 10 per cent for 2022 in winemag's review, so the record says a modest share; nine months in barrel rests on the house's Seven Flags page and winemag.
The ageing is the author's reading; the Riesling and Noble Late Harvest in others come from the Codex's region record, not from a search of this run.

records.place: Near Grabouw, Elgin district, Cape South Coast region

wine.name: Oak Valley Pinot Noir Groenlandberg
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir, all of it, from several clones grown on the estate.
wine.sites: Estate vineyards high on the southern slopes of the Groenland mountain, at roughly three hundred to four hundred and thirty metres, on Bokkeveld shale rich in clay.
wine.making: Fermented with a share of whole bunches and matured in French oak barrels, in the 2023 vintage about ten months with roughly a third of the barrels new, before the clones and parcels are blended and bottled.
wine.glass: Red cherry, strawberry and red apple with rose petal, tea leaf and a hint of cinnamon, light and fresh, with silky, fine tannin and a tart, salty finish.
wine.ageing: Bright and open young, it shows well in its first five to eight years, and a cool vintage gains from two or three years of rest.
wine.serve: 12 to 15 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The mountain above the farm, on whose slopes the fruit grows; a name, not an appellation.
Grown in the Elgin district of the Cape South Coast region.

records.table: Oak Valley grows its Groenlandberg Pinot Noir high on the shale slopes of the Groenland mountain above Elgin's orchards, with a share of whole bunches and French oak. It is light and fresh: red cherry, rose and tea leaf over fine tannin.
records.story: Oak Valley was founded in December 1898, when Sir Antonie Viljoen (1858 to 1918), a doctor trained at Edinburgh and later a member of the Cape's upper house, bought a large, undeveloped stretch of farmland near Grabouw. By the house's account he planted the first commercial apple and pear orchards of the Elgin valley, and he planted vines too: in 1907 he built a cellar and pressed his first grapes, and by 1918 the farm held about a hundred thousand vines. Demand for wine fell during the Second World War, and in 1944 the cellar was closed. Wine came back in the mid 1980s, in step with the Cluver family's venture on the neighbouring farm: an experimental block of eight varieties gave its first harvest in the summer of 1988, and its Pinot Noir showed promise. In 1992 new vineyards of Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir went in on the south facing slopes, and for some years their fruit went to Bouchard Finlayson in Walker Bay. The wines were later made at Paul Cluver, until the estate's own winery was finished in time for the 2017 harvest. The Groenlandberg Pinot Noir carries both the farm and its mountain: Elgin red that is about freshness, not weight.

others.name: Oak Valley Groenlandberg Chardonnay
others.note: The white twin of the flagship, from the same mountain, and its equal in the house's range.

others.name: Oak Valley Sounds of Silence Pinot Noir
others.note: Pinot Noir from a high, isolated vineyard in the Groenland foothills.

others.name: Oak Valley Tabula Rasa
others.note: Single vineyard, single clone Chardonnay and Pinot Noir made in small batches.

traps: Groenlandberg names the mountain above the farm, not a ward or an appellation; the appellation on the label is Wine of Origin Elgin.
Oak Valley is a fruit and wine farm of 1898, yet its own modern winery dates only from the 2017 harvest; the wines were made at Paul Cluver before that.

cards.front: Oak Valley: who founded it, and when?
cards.back: Sir Antonie Viljoen, a doctor and Cape politician, in December 1898.

cards.front: On what soil does Oak Valley grow its Groenlandberg Pinot Noir?
cards.back: Bokkeveld shale rich in clay, high on the slopes of the Groenland mountain.

questions.q: A guest asks what Groenlandberg means on a bottle of Oak Valley Pinot Noir. Which answer fits?
opts: The mountain whose slopes give the fruit
A classified ward of the Elgin district
The founder's family name in Dutch
A clone of Pinot Noir from Dijon
questions.exp: It is the Groenland mountain above the farm, where the vineyards lie; the appellation is Wine of Origin Elgin, not a ward named Groenlandberg.

questions.q: Oak Valley's modern wines were long made at a neighbour's cellar. With which harvest did its own new winery begin?
questions.exp: The estate winery was finished in time for the 2017 harvest; 1992 is the planting on the south facing slopes and 1988 the harvest of the experimental block.

report: The plan's Oak Valley Pinot Noir is sold as the Groenlandberg Pinot Noir on the house's sheets and at The Wine Society; the name is written Oak Valley Pinot Noir Groenlandberg, the order Decanter uses for the pair, to keep the plan's words; no renaming was found.

Which wine heads the range is open: the house names its Groenlandberg Chardonnay and Pinot Noir as a pair and gives neither as the flagship, and its Chardonnay has the louder awards; no swap is proposed, but the checker may weigh the Groenlandberg Chardonnay.

The cellar is 1907 on the house's pages and 1908 in one other account; 1907 is kept. The cooperation with the Cluver family dates from 1985 in the house's history on winemag, against 1987 on the Cluver side, so the story says the mid 1980s.

Ten months in barrel and about a third new rest on winemag's review of the 2023 vintage alone and are hedged as one recent vintage; the house's own sheet gives whole bunches and French oak without figures.
The founder's dates rest on Wikipedia and the house's history; his knighthood of 1916, his purchase price and the claim that he studied beside Arthur Conan Doyle are left out.
The ageing is the author's reading. Living members of the family and the winemakers are not named.

records.place: The high plateau of the Elgin district, Cape South Coast region

wine.name: Iona Sauvignon Blanc
wine.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, the great majority, with a small share of Sémillon.
wine.sites: Nine blocks on the farm's high ground at about four hundred and twenty metres, on former apple country close to the cold Atlantic, cooled by sea breezes and summer cloud.
wine.making: Each of the nine blocks is picked and made apart. The Sauvignon Blanc is fermented in stainless steel and rests on its lees in tank for some months, while the small part of Sémillon is fermented naturally in older French oak barrels of five hundred litres; there is no new oak.
wine.glass: Gooseberry, lime and green apple with pear and grapefruit, a chalky, flinty edge and racy acidity, delicate rather than loud, with a long, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Fresh and open on release, it gains texture over two to four years, and a good vintage keeps for five years or more.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass of medium size.

label.means: The house's name for its estate range from the high lying farm.
Grown in the Elgin district of the Cape South Coast region.

records.table: Iona grows its Sauvignon Blanc at about four hundred and twenty metres above Elgin, within reach of the Atlantic's cool air, and adds a little Sémillon fermented in old oak. It is pale and delicate, with gooseberry, lime and a flinty edge.
records.story: In 1997 a businessman bought a run down apple farm on high ground above the Elgin valley and named it Iona, after the Scottish island of his forebears. Ground that had not suited apples went to vines, and in 1998 the first were planted, Sauvignon Blanc first among them. With no cellar of its own, the farm made its first wine in 2001, a Sauvignon Blanc, and the house dates every vintage since from that year. The farm lies at about four hundred and twenty metres, close to the cold Atlantic, under the cloud and wind of summer, and the house calls it one of the cooler vineyard sites of the country. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir followed, from vines of 2003 and 2009, and on Brocha, a biodynamic farm of the house, red varieties were planted in 2004 and first made in 2007. In 2022 the house marked its twenty first vintage. Through all of it the Sauvignon Blanc has stayed the wine most guests meet first, bottled under the Elgin Highlands name. It shows what height and sea air do to the grape in the Cape: a pale, chalky, restrained wine rather than a loud one.

others.name: Iona Elgin Highlands Wild Ferment Sauvignon Blanc
others.note: A fuller Sauvignon Blanc with Sémillon, fermented with wild yeasts and given time in barrel before tank.

others.name: Iona Elgin Highlands Chardonnay
others.note: Chardonnay from blocks such as Kloof and Kraal, from vines planted in 2003 and 2009.

others.name: Iona Kroon Pinot Noir
others.note: Single vineyard Pinot Noir from the farm's Kroon block.

traps: Iona's first vintage is 2001; 1997 is the year the apple farm was bought and 1998 the year of its first vines.
The Elgin Highlands Sauvignon Blanc is mostly tank made with a small part of barrel fermented Sémillon; the Wild Ferment bottling is a separate, fuller wine.

Long ageing in new French oak barriques
Old bush vines on warm Swartland granite
Late picking for richness and sweetness
questions.exp: The farm sits at about four hundred and twenty metres close to the Atlantic, so the season is cool and long; the wine sees no new oak and is not late picked.

questions.q: In which year did Iona make its first wine, a Sauvignon Blanc?
questions.exp: The house's wine began with 2001; 1997 is the purchase of the farm, 1998 the first planting and 2004 the reds on Brocha.

report: The house's shop names the wine Elgin Highlands Sauvignon Blanc and The Wine Society Iona Sauvignon Blanc, Elgin; the record keeps the plan's Iona Sauvignon Blanc and gives Elgin Highlands as a label term.
The buyer of 1997 is living and not named; his trade is a medical suture business in one account and engineering in another, so the story says a businessman.
The crush of the first vintage at a Stellenbosch cellar rests on one source and is left out; 1997, 1998 and 2001 rest on the house's page, The Drinks Business, BizNews and Wine Anorak.
The Sémillon share is about 5 per cent and five months on the gross lees in the house's note for 2024, and the share has moved over the years, so the record says a small share and some months.
The Codex's region record calls the farm high lying, which agrees; the house calls itself the highest winery in Elgin, which is not repeated. The ageing is the author's reading.
No swap proposed: the Sauvignon Blanc is the wine the house is best known by abroad, though its Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are made with equal care.

records.place: Above the Peninsula Dam, Elgin district, Cape South Coast region

wine.name: Mount Bullet Merlot
wine.grapes: Merlot, all of it, from five clones grown in one vineyard.
wine.sites: A single Merlot vineyard on a mountain hillside above the Peninsula Dam, on Table Mountain sandstone rich in quartz over a deeper base of kaolin clay.
wine.making: Each of the five clones is fermented with wild yeasts and matured apart, in French barriques from several Bordeaux cooperages, for about twenty months, a quarter to two fifths of them new in the vintages reviewed, before the parts are blended and bottled.
wine.glass: Red and black berries, violet and pencil shavings with dried herbs, damp earth and a little leafiness, dense and powerful, with firm but fine tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Firm when young, it wants four or five years in bottle and lasts beyond a decade in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The name the house gives its single vineyard Merlot.
Grown in the Elgin district of the Cape South Coast region.

records.table: Shannon's Mount Bullet Merlot comes from one hillside vineyard above the Peninsula Dam in Elgin, its five clones made apart and aged for many months in French barriques. It is dark and firm, with berries, violet and pencil shavings.
records.story: Shannon Vineyards takes its name from the family's Irish roots. Its farm lies in the Elgin valley, long the apple and pear country of the Cape, on mountain hillsides above the banks of the Peninsula Dam, and the family set it up as a wine farm in 2000, the year of its oldest Pinot Noir vineyard by the house's account. Two brothers of the family run it, one of them a careful grower of the vines, and the wines are made with outside winemakers rather than by a cellar team of the house's own. Merlot is the grape the farm is known by. The house calls the Mount Bullet vineyard the oldest Merlot vineyard of the valley, and it is planted to five different clones on sandstone and clay. Each parcel is fermented and matured on its own, in barriques from several Bordeaux cooperages, for about twenty months, before the five are blended into Mount Bullet. From the 2013 vintage one clone of the vineyard was also bottled on its own, as Shannon Black. Mount Bullet shows a cool district that is famous for white wine and Pinot Noir making Merlot of depth and firmness, from slopes where the season runs long and slow.

others.name: Shannon Black
others.note: A single clone Merlot from the Mount Bullet vineyard, bottled on its own from the 2013 vintage.

others.name: Shannon Elgin Merlot

traps: Shannon Vineyards of Elgin is a South African family farm; it has nothing to do with Shannon Family of Wines in Lake County, California.
Mount Bullet is all Merlot from five clones blended; Shannon Black is a single clone of the same vineyard bottled on its own.

report: Founded 2000 rests on two listings (Winemaps and a Virgin Wines page) and the house's date for its oldest Pinot Noir block; the house's own about page was not read, so the checker may confirm it or empty the field.

The first vintage of Mount Bullet was not found: listings run back to 2007, which is not shown to be the first, so no first vintage is given. What the name Mount Bullet refers to was not found either.

The story that a viticulturist persuaded the family's father not to pull out the low yielding Merlot block, which became Mount Bullet, rests on one column whose address names a living writer, so it is left out; the father is not named.

Twenty months in barriques of three Bordeaux cooperages rests on winemag's 2013 review and the same column, and Decanter gives twenty months and a quarter new for 2016; a house note of nine months in old oak belongs, as far as could be told, to the Elgin Merlot.
The brothers who own the farm and the winemakers who make the wines are living and not named; that the winemakers are outside the house rests on listings and reviews.
The ageing and serving are the author's reading; the line that Elgin is known for whites and Pinot Noir follows the Codex's region record.

records.place: Elgin district, Cape South Coast region, from bought Elgin fruit

wine.name: Kershaw Clonal Selection Elgin Chardonnay
wine.grapes: Chardonnay, all of it, blended from Dijon clones CY95, CY96, CY76 and CY548.
wine.sites: Small parcels across Elgin, eleven of them in 2023, chosen clone by clone and soil by soil from growers' vineyards; the house owns no vines of its own.
wine.making: Whole bunch pressed, each clone and soil type is made as its own small batch in French oak barrels of 228 litres, about a third of them new, and the wine rests in barrel for some ten to eleven months before blending and bottling.
wine.glass: Lemon and toast with a hint of matchstick, a taut, precise line and fresh green herbs, pure fruit and lively, juicy acidity, with real structure and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Taut on release, it opens after three to five years in bottle and should keep for a decade or more.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though air helps a young bottle; a Burgundy white glass.

label.means: The house's blend of several Chardonnay clones, above the single clone Deconstructed wines.
Grown in the Elgin district of the Cape South Coast region.

records.table: Kershaw's Clonal Selection Elgin Chardonnay is built from four Dijon clones grown in small Elgin parcels, each made apart in French barrels before the blend. It is taut and precise: lemon, toast and a hint of matchstick on lively acidity.
records.story: Richard Kershaw Wines is the house of a winemaker who travelled widely before settling in the Cape in 1999 to make wine full time, and who passed the Master of Wine examination in September 2011. In January 2012 the founder started the house, and its first wine was a Chardonnay from Elgin of that same vintage, a solo venture that critics in Britain and South Africa greeted warmly. The house is a virtual winery by its own description: it owns no vineyards, buying grapes from Elgin growers and hiring cellar space to make the wine. What sets it apart is its study of clones and soils. The Clonal Selection Chardonnay blends Dijon clones, CY95, CY96, CY76 and the CY548 of the French nursery body, from small parcels picked and made apart, and the Deconstructed range bottles a single clone from a single soil, so that the drinker can taste each piece of the blend on its own. A Clonal Selection Syrah from Elgin later joined the Chardonnay in the range. Its Clonal Selection Chardonnay is the wine to learn first: the sum of the parts the Deconstructed wines take apart.

others.name: Kershaw Deconstructed Chardonnay
others.note: Single clone, single soil Chardonnays, such as CY96 from Bokkeveld shale, each a part of the blend bottled alone.

others.name: Kershaw Clonal Selection Elgin Syrah
others.note: The house's Syrah from Elgin, built from clones in the same way.

traps: The house buys its fruit and owns no vineyards; Kershaw is a virtual winery, not an estate.
The Clonal Selection is a blend of clones; the Deconstructed wines each show one clone from one soil, and are not the flagship blend.

cards.front: Kershaw Clonal Selection Elgin Chardonnay: which clones go into the blend?
cards.back: Dijon clones CY95, CY96, CY76 and CY548.

cards.front: Richard Kershaw Wines: when was the house started, and what was its first wine?
cards.back: January 2012; an Elgin Chardonnay of the 2012 vintage.

questions.q: A guest asks how the Kershaw Clonal Selection Chardonnay differs from the Deconstructed wines. Which answer fits?
opts: It blends several clones; each Deconstructed wine is one clone
It is unoaked; the Deconstructed wines see new oak
It comes from Stellenbosch; the Deconstructed wines from Elgin
It is a sweet wine; the Deconstructed wines are dry
questions.exp: The Clonal Selection is the blend of four Dijon clones; the Deconstructed range bottles single clones from single soils. Both are oaked Elgin Chardonnay.

questions.q: What kind of house is Richard Kershaw Wines, by its own description?
opts: A virtual winery that buys grapes and hires cellar space
An old fruit farm with vines planted in 1898
A co-operative cellar of Elgin apple growers
A family estate on its own farm since 1896
questions.exp: It owns no vineyards, buying fruit and renting cellar room; the old farms of 1898 and 1896 are Oak Valley and Paul Cluver.

report: The founder is living and is never named in prose; the house's name keeps his surname, as the brief allows. The plan's Elgin Chardonnay is sold as the Clonal Selection Elgin Chardonnay, which the name gives.

Founded 2012 rests on the house's About page and Berry Bros; the 2012 first vintage on Wine Anorak and a Platter's note quoted in search. The founder's earlier posts at Mulderbosch and Kanu rest on one listing and are left out.

The clone list and eleven parcels are the house's for 2023; ten months and whole bunch pressing are its notes for 2015, so making says ten to eleven months; the new oak was 34 per cent in 2023 and 50 per cent in 2022 by one critic's note, so about a third is hedged.
The house describes itself as a virtual winery, buying grapes and hiring cellar space; where it makes the wine is not given.
The glass rests on Wine Anorak's note on the 2012 and reviews of 2016 and 2020 as summarised in search; it is the author's synthesis across vintages, as is the ageing.
Richard's Elgin Chardonnay, sold through Naked Wines and reviewed by Decanter, is a separate bottling and is not the flagship. The Codex's region record does not list the house.
